## Which observations are in the middle? {#l2-middle-position .middle-position}

First **order the data**. For $n$ observations, calculate

$$\text{middle position}=\frac{n+1}{2}.$$

::: {.split}
::: {.column-block}
<h3>If the result is an integer</h3>

The median is the **value at that position**.

For $n=9$:

$$\frac{9+1}{2}=5.$$

Use the **5th value**.
:::
::: {.column-block}
<h3>If the result ends in .5</h3>

Average the **values at the positions immediately below and above**.

For $n=10$:

$$\frac{10+1}{2}=5.5.$$

Average the **5th and 6th values**.
:::
:::

<p class="small-note">An integer result occurs when <span data-math="n">n</span> is odd; a .5 result occurs when <span data-math="n">n</span> is even. The calculation locates the middle—it does not give the median value.</p>

::: notes
Use (n+1)/2 as the single locating rule, with the parentheses explicit. An integer result identifies one position; a result ending in .5 lies halfway between two positions. Average the two data values at those positions, not the position numbers themselves. Apply this next to n=50 in the pet table: (50+1)/2=25.5, so read positions 25 and 26. Both contain the value 1. This explanation replaces the former 'Locate before calculating' slide.
:::
